criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and municipal drinking-water supply and wastewater/sanitation service access across Stockholm County and specifically in Norrtälje municipality, comparing central municipal network connections, co-ownership mini-networks, and autonomous individual wells/septic systems, as well as seasonal ('summer water') versus permanent year-round supply.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it analyses local municipal water/wastewater policies, urban planning governance, intermunicipal utility associations, Veolia's operational concession, and the 2007 Swedish Water Act. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access and cost allocation: (1) statutory full cost-recovery ('principe du prix coûtant'), municipal tariff equalization ('péréquation municipale'), connection fee rules (~70,000 vs. ~150,000 SEK/house), and the 2007 Water Act rule authorizing cost-differentiated intra-municipal tariffs; (2) administrative classification of 122 residential zones into municipal connection versus alternative-system tiers; (3) unanimous co-owner consent requirements and bonus building-right incentives for co-ownership mini-networks (minimum 20 houses); and (4) permitting and enforcement rules, including municipal environmental authorization/registration fees for individual systems, mandatory adequate sanitation upgrades triggered by building-permit applications to convert summerhouses into permanent residences, and statutory municipal obligations to enforce remediation or connect properties when autonomous systems pose environmental hazards.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative and descriptive case study combining primary stakeholder interviews (Regional Planning Office/RTK, Käppalaförbundet CEO, Norrtälje head of water and wastewater Bertil Rusk, and former mayor Håkan Jonsson), municipal planning/programme documents and public meeting records, and municipal/utility statistical data from Svenskt Vatten (VASS) and Statistics Sweden (SCB). Per protocol safeguards, qualitative socio-legal/governance empirical studies are eligible even without quantitative effect-size estimation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access, connection, availability, and affordability/cost outcomes: municipal drinking-water and wastewater network connection rates across 26 municipalities (e.g., 56.07%/57.5% connected vs. 42.5%/44% off-network in Norrtälje; ~90,000 off-network households county-wide), seasonal 6-month 'summer water' vs. permanent supply, uptake of co-ownership mini-networks (~50 cases / 1,000 residences), annual household tariffs for apartments and houses across 26 municipalities, volumetric rate increases (21.40 to 24.50 SEK/m3), connection charges (~70,000 vs. ~150,000 SEK/house), and 40%-50% cost differentials cross-subsidized through uniform municipal tariffs.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (26 Stockholm County municipalities; 122 residential zones and permanent/seasonal households in Norrtälje), legal/regulatory and tariff exposures, access/connection/tariff outcomes, and empirical case-study design are all clearly identifiable from the text.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in French (with embedded English primary interview quotes). Per Inclusion Criterion 10 and Checklist item 6, studies in languages other than English, Portuguese, or Dutch are eligible when translation from the provided full text is feasible and the study is mechanism-relevant; direct translation from this clean machine-readable French text is fully feasible and should be logged in extraction_note during data extraction.

study_design: Qualitative and descriptive empirical case study (stakeholder interviews, municipal planning/policy document analysis, and utility/municipal administrative statistics)
population_and_sample: 26 municipalities of Stockholm County (~2 million residents, including ~90,000 off-network households), with an in-depth case study of Norrtälje municipality (55,530 permanent residents, 25,000-30,000 secondary summerhouses, and 122 residential zones)
exposure: Statutory full cost-recovery and municipal tariff equalization/differentiation rules (2007 Swedish Water Act), municipal zoning/eligibility screening across four service/ownership tiers (122 zones), unanimous co-owner consent and fee-sharing rules for co-ownership mini-networks, building-permit sanitation upgrade mandates upon converting secondary summerhouses into permanent residences, and environmental permitting/mandatory network connection enforcement
outcome: Municipal and household drinking-water and wastewater network connection rates vs. reliance on co-ownership mini-networks or autonomous on-site systems, seasonal ('summer water') vs. year-round water availability, and household connection charges, annual tariffs, and intra-municipal cross-subsidization
rationale: This French-language empirical case study (eligible under Criterion 10 with feasible translation from the clean full text) examines household and municipal water and sanitation access across Stockholm County and in Norrtälje, Sweden. It satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2 by analysing statutory full cost-recovery and municipal tariff equalization/differentiation rules under the 2007 Water Act, zone-level connection screening, unanimous co-owner consent and connection-fee rules for co-ownership mini-networks, building-permit sanitation mandates triggered by converting summerhouses to permanent residences, and mandatory municipal connection enforcement when off-network systems cause environmental harm. Drawing on stakeholder interviews, municipal planning records, and Svenskt Vatten (VASS) data, it reports concrete connection coverage, seasonal vs. year-round availability, and tariff/connection-cost outcomes.
